## Slide 2: Problem Solving
Problem Solving
An Important application of Artificial intelligence is problem solving.
Problem solving agent with several immediate options of unknown value can decide what to do by just examining different possible sequence of actions that lead to state of known values, and then choosing the best sequence.

## Slide 3: Problem-Solving Agents
Problem-Solving Agents
Goal Based Agent
Agent adopt a goal and aim at satisfying them.
Goals help organize behavior by limiting the objectives that the agent is trying to achieve and hence the actions it needs to consider.
It will consider a long sequence of possible actions before deciding whether the goal is achieved.
These sequence of actions lead to the desired goal.
A Problem Solving agent ,with several immediate options of unknown value can decide what to do by first examining future actions that eventually lead to  states of known value

Properties of the Environment
Observable: agent always knows the current state.
Discrete: at any given state there are only finitely many actions to 	choose from .
Known: agent knows which states are reached by each action.
Deterministic: each action has exactly one outcome.

## Slide 6: Goal Formulation
Goal Formulation
First step in problem solving is goal formulation
It organizes finite steps to formulate a target/goals which require some action to achieve the goal.
It is based on the current situation and the agent’s performance measure
The goal is formulated
as a set of world states, in which the goal is satisfied
Reaching from initial state         goal state
Actions are required
Actions are the operators
causing transitions between world states
Actions should be abstract enough at a certain degree, instead of very detailed
◦ E.g., turn left VS turn left 30 degree, etc.
With such high level of detail there is too much uncertainty in the world and there would be too many steps in a solution for agent to find a solution

## Slide 9: Well-defined problems and solutions
Well-defined problems and solutions
A problem can be defined formally by following components:
1. The initial state that the agent starts in .
eg:In(Arad)
2. A description of the possible actions available to the agent.
Uses a successor function. Given a particular state x, Successor Function returns a set of ordered pair<action,successor>
where each action is one of the legal actions in state x and each successor is a state that can be reached from x by applying the action.
From the state In(Arad) ,successor function returns
{<Go(Sibiu),In(Sibiu>,< Go(Timisoara),In(Timisoara >,< Go(Zerind),In(Zerind >}
This Initial state and Successor function implicitly define the State space

## Slide 10: A path in the state space is a sequence of states connected by a sequence of actions
A path in the state space is a sequence of states connected by a sequence of actions
The goal test, which determines whether a given state is a goal state
{In(Bucharest)}
A path cost function that assigns a numeric cost to each path. cost of a path can be described as the sum of the costs of the individual actions along the path.
The step cost of taking action a in state x to reach state y is denoted by c(x, a, y ).
A solution to a problem is an action sequence that leads from the initial state to a goal state. Solution quality is measured by the path cost function, and an optimal solution has the lowest path cost among all solutions

## Slide 11: Search
Search
The process of looking for a sequence of actions that reaches the goal is called search.
A search algorithm takes a problem as input and returns a solution in the form of an action sequence .
Once a solution is found, the actions it recommends can be carried out. This is called the execution phase

6714386db10dec985fc8.text:

## Slide 12: Searching Process
Searching Process
1. Formulate a goal and a problem to solve,
2. the agent calls a search procedure to solve it
3. Agent uses the solution to guide its actions,
4. do whatever the solution recommends
5. remove that step from the sequence.
6. Once the solution has been executed, the agent will formulate a new 	goal.

Open-loop system
while the agent is executing the solution sequence it ignores its percepts when choosing an action because it knows in advance what they will be
An agent that carries out its plans with its eyes closed, so to speak, must be quite certain of what is going on is an open loop.
ignoring the percepts breaks the loop between agent and environment.

## Slide 27: There are two main kinds of formulation
There are two main kinds of formulation
An incremental formulation
involves operators that augment the state description starting from an empty state
Each action adds a queen to the state
States: any arrangement of 0 to 8 queens on board
Successor function: add a queen to any empty square
A complete-state formulation
starts with all 8 queens on the board
move the queens individually around
States: any arrangement of 8 queens, one per column in the leftmost columns
Operators: move an attacked queen to a row, not attacked by any other
the right formulation makes a big difference to the size of the search space

## Slide 70: A variant of depth-first search called backtracking search uses still less memory.
A variant of depth-first search called backtracking search uses still less memory.
In backtracking, only one successor is generated at a time rather than all successors;
each partially expanded node remembers which successor to generate next. In this way, only O(m) memory is needed rather than O(bm).
Backtracking search facilitates yet another memory-saving (and time-saving) trick:
the idea of generating a successor by modifying the current state description directly rather than copying it first. This reduces the memory requirements to just one state description and O(m) actions.

## Slide 98: The first condition we require for optimality is that h(n) be an admissible heuristic.
The first condition we require for optimality is that h(n) be an admissible heuristic.
An admissible heuristic is one that never overestimates the cost to reach the goal.
g(n) is the actual cost to reach n along the current path, and
f(n) = g(n) + h(n), we have as an immediate consequence that f(n) never overestimates the true cost of a solution along the current path through n.
Admissible heuristics are by nature optimistic because they think the cost of solving the problem is less than it actually is
◦ Eg, straight-line distance hSLD that we used in getting to Bucharest is n admissible heuristic
◦ because the shortest path between any two points is a straight line
◦ Straight line cannot be an overestimate

## Slide 99: Conditions for optimality: Consistency
Conditions for optimality: Consistency
It is required only for applications of A∗ to graph search
A heuristic h(n) is consistent if, for every node n and every successor n of n generated by any action a, the estimated cost of reaching the goal from n is no greater than the step cost of getting to n plus the estimated cost of reaching the goal from n :
h(n) ≤ c(n, a, n’ ) + h(n’ )
This is a form of the general triangle inequality, which stipulates that each side of a triangle cannot be longer than the sum of the other two sides
◦ Here, the triangle is formed by n, n , and the goal Gn closest to n.
◦ For an admissible heuristic, the inequality makes perfect sense:
if there were a route from n to Gn via n that was cheaper than h(n), that would violate the property that h(n) is a lower bound on the cost to reach Gn.

## Slide 100: Optimality of A*
Optimality of A*
the tree-search version of A∗ is optimal if h(n) is admissible, while the graph-search version is optimal if h(n) is consistent.
A∗ expands no nodes with f(n) > C∗—
C∗ is the cost of the optimal solution path
for example, Timisoara is not expanded in even though it is a child of the root
the subtree below Timisoara is pruned; because hSLD is admissible, the algorithm can safely ignore this subtree while still guaranteeing optimality
Pruning eliminates possibilities from consideration without having to examine them
A∗ is optimally efficient for any given consistent heuristic.
◦ That is, no other optimal algorithm is guaranteed to expand fewer nodes than A∗
◦ This is because any algorithm that does not expand all nodes with f(n) < C∗ runs the risk of missing the optimal solution.

## Slide 101: if h(n) is consistent, then the values of f(n) along any path are nondecreasing.
if h(n) is consistent, then the values of f(n) along any path are nondecreasing.
The proof follows directly from the definition of consistency.
Suppose n is a successor of n; then g(n ) = g(n) + c(n, a, n ) for some action a, and we have
f(n ) = g(n ) + h(n ) = g(n) + c(n, a, n ) + h(n ) ≥ g(n) + h(n) = f(n) .

## Slide 103: Admissible Heuristics
Admissible Heuristics
h1 = the number of misplaced tiles.
For Figure 3.28, all of the eight tiles are out of position, so the start state would have h1 = 8. h1 is an admissible heuristic because it is clear that any tile that is out of place must be moved at least once.
• h2 = the sum of the distances of the tiles from their goal positions. Because tiles cannot move along diagonals, the distance we will count is the sum of the horizontal and vertical distances. This is sometimes called the city block distance or Manhattan distance.
h2 is also admissible because all any move can do is move one tile one step closer to the goal.
Tiles 1 to 8 in the start state give a Manhattan distance of
◦ h2 = 3 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 18

[Context: tmpmgcah9ns.pptx > tmpmgcah9ns > Slide 104: Quality of Heuristics]
## Slide 104: Quality of Heuristics
Quality of Heuristics
Since A* expands all nodes whose f value is less than that of an optimal solution, it is always better to use a heuristic with a higher value as long as it does not over-estimate.
Therefore h2 is uniformly better than h1 , or h2 dominates h1 .
A heuristic should also be easy to compute, otherwise the overhead of computing the heuristic could outweigh the time saved by reducing search (e.g. using full breadth-first search to estimate distance wouldn’t help)

Abstract— Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for gait analy-
sis utilizing Vertical Ground Reaction Force (VGRF) signals
have demonstrated signiﬁcant potential in Parkinson’s
Disease (PD) diagnosis and rehabilitation ﬁelds. How-
ever, existing GNN-based methods in this area normally
model the VGRF signals as static topological structures,
and ignore the dynamic variations of the VGRF graph
structures during walking. To address this issue, a Global-
Local Dynamic Directed Graph Neural Network (GLD2-GNN)
is proposed to represent the dynamic spatio-temporal
features of VGRF signals.

types of approaches to model dynamic graphs: discrete-time
and continuous-time approaches [25]. Discrete-time approaches typically represent a dynamic

this section, detailed experimental content will be introduced,
including experimental setup, ablation experiments, and com-
parison with existing methods.

conditions. These datasets encompass VGRF records of 93
Parkinson’s Disease patients and 73 healthy controls, which
are obtained by asking the subjects to walk for approximately
two minutes at the comfortable speed.

The setting of hyper-parameters of our method is as follows. The model mainly consists of four DyDGNN blocks and a
classiﬁcation block. The input channels for the four DyDGNN
blocks are conﬁgured as 1, 32, 32, and 64 respectively. During
training, the Adam optimizer is used with β1 = 0.9, β2 =
0.995, and a weight decay of 5e-4. The training iteration is
120. The initial learning rate is 5e-4, which is adjusted by
CosineAnnealingLR strategy with a period of 14 epochs and
a minimum value of 1e-5. The batch size is 64 and entropy
loss is applied. To prevent overﬁtting, 80% of each training set is used
for the model training, and the remaining 20% is utilized
as the validation set to apply an early stopping strategy
with a patience of 30, where random seeds do not follow
speciﬁc selection rules.

Since many diseases exhibit distinct motor symptoms and
gait characteristics, we believe that our framework based on
VGRF signals can be applied for detecting other diseases with
motor symptoms. In practical applications, our framework can
be applied to the detection tasks of other diseases through
some adjustments. First, it is necessary to select the appropri-
ate data processing methods for the detection task. Moreover,
if the topological structure of plantar pressure signals in other
diseases exhibits signiﬁcant di ﬀerences from the predeﬁned
graph structure of this manuscript, it is important to recon-
struct the topological relationships of VGRF signals based
on the pathological characteristics of the diseases. Notably,
GLD2-GNN introduces dynamic graph learning and dynamic
topological feature fusion, which are applicable to other
neurodegenerative disease data with topological relationships

to optimize the model’s performance in high-load scenarios

VI. C ONCLUSION
In this paper, we treat VGRF signals as a type of data
with dynamic graph structure, and propose GLD 2-GNN to
exploit the topological characteristics of VGRF signals. The
Dynamic Graph Learning (DGL) unit is proposed to learn
dynamic topological relationships of VGRF signals. Based
on learned graphs, GLD 2-GNN generates dynamic features. Subsequently, a Dynamic Directed Graph Network (DyDGN)
unit and a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) unit are
constructed to aggregate the dynamic features and capture gait
patterns of VGRF signals. By modeling topological evolution
of the VGRF signals and extracting spatio-temporal patterns,

Context-Aware Retrieval Augmented Generation
Using Similarity Validation to Handle Context
Inconsistencies in Large Language Models
ENRICO COLLINI
, FELIX INDRA KURNIADI, PAOLO NESI
 , (Life Member, IEEE),
AND GIANNI PANTALEO
Distributed Systems and Internet Technologies Laboratory (DISIT Lab), Department of Information Engineering, University of Florence, 50139 Florence, Italy
Corresponding author: Paolo Nesi (paolo.nesi@unifi.it)
This work was supported by the Ministry University of Research (MUR), project CAI4DSA of FAIR PE1.
ABSTRACT Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed natural language processing by offering
human-like responses. However, issues such as incorrect information (hallucinations) and errors in specific
subject areas remain, especially in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. This study introduces
a Context-Aware Retrieval Augmented Generation (CA-RAG), which simplifies the process by removing
the need to separately find relevant chunks of a document. Instead, after dividing the document into
chunks, both the question and chunks are directly given to the LLMs to produce answers. The method then
focuses on improving the answers through additional post-processing, aiming to reduce errors and make the

focuses on improving the answers through additional post-processing, aiming to reduce errors and make the
answers more relevant to the question. To evaluate the effectiveness of CA-RAG, two scenarios have been
designed. Scenario 1 involved experiments using widely adopted and recognized benchmark datasets, such
as TriviaQA, Natural Questions, AmbigQA and Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD). In this
context, the proposed CA-RAG method, combined with similarity measure (either cosine similarity or dot
product) between generated answers and chunks, achieved the highest F1-score in TriviaQA and AmbigQA. Scenario 2 tested CA-RAG robustness using a custom dataset comprising domain-specific and unstructured
documents. Results from automated and manual evaluations revealed that CA-RAG with post-processing
consistently outperformed traditional RAG. These findings highlight the critical role of post-processing
techniques and similarity measures in improving the accuracy and relevance of generated answers. CA-
RAG demonstrates strong potential as a reliable and versatile solution for Retrieval Augmented Generation
tasks across diverse datasets and domains.

important developments in Artificial Intelligence. LLMs like
ChatGPT [1], Claude [2], and Llama [3] can create text with
strong ‘‘understanding’’ and answers to questions in ways
that make sense to humans. These models use deep neural
networks trained on large amounts of text data, which allows
them to understand and produce human-like language.

For these
reasons, fine-tuning may not be the best approach in all those
cases and contexts in which users, research entities, organiza-
tions and companies require to build LLM-based applications
and services for specific domain knowledge (products and/or
services manuals, internal/legal documentation etc.) which
may need frequent or continuous updates. To address these challenges, the Retrieval-Augmented
Generation (RAG) approach [16] has been considered. This
method improves LLM performance by retrieving relevant
information from pre-existing documents and using it to
generate answers. In this way, the RAG approach reduces
the need for exhaustive fine-tuning by leveraging up-to-
date information and specific domain knowledge, therefore
minimizing computational overhead and related costs. RAG
combines two processes:
1) Retrieval: The system retrieves relevant information
from external documents or sources. 2) Generation: The retrieved information is then used to
generate responses based on the query.

RAG is designed to use context for specific tasks, enabling
it to generate more relevant and tailored outputs in Question
and Answer tasks on specific domain knowledge. Therefore,
RAG allows to handle queries that go beyond the scope of
pre-trained models, since it excels at managing specialized
domain knowledge retrieved from external sources [21]. Moreover, RAG minimizes the risk of data leakage from
the pre-trained model, making it a reliable option for
maintaining privacy [22]. Furthermore, while fine-tuning
offers consistent performance, RAG provides a more efficient
and cost-effective alternative [23]. However, while efficient,
the traditional RAG approach introduces a critical bottleneck:
the overall answer quality heavily depends on the retriever’s
performance, as well as on the precision of the contextual
information used to generate answers [24]. Previous research
has identified computational complexity [21], [25] and
retrieval challenges [26], [27] as significant weaknesses in
current RAG. In particular, similarity measures used in the
retrieval stage may not effectively capture the contextual
relevance between a query and potentially relevant docu-
ments [28], [29]. Furthermore, dense vector representations,

chunks which may be lexically similar but semantically
misaligned with the user’s expectations. Therefore, despite
its many advantages, traditional RAG has several significant
limitations. In order to address all the described issues,
this study proposes the Context-Aware Retrieval Augmented
Generation (CA-RAG) solution. B. PROPOSED METHOD AND CONTRIBUTIONS
The CA-RAG approach focuses on improving context aware-
ness and mitigating retrieval precision issues by eliminating
the retrieval initial filter. Rather than ranking raw documents
based on vector similarity to the query, our proposed method
consists in performing semantic chunking on documents
and providing all the extracted chunks to the LLM to
generate answers. Then, we rank generated answers using
similarity methods between the generated text and the
context, discarding answers whose similarity score undergoes
a certain threshold. This new approach moves the relevance

Pickett et al. [25] suggested a novel paradigm named
Dartboard. This study introduces the Dartboard algorithm,
which uses a simple measure of total information gain
for a specific query, and evaluates the effectiveness of
Dartboard on the RAG Benchmark. Their system was
compared with other methods including Oracle, Maximal
Marginal Relevance (MMR) Crosscoder, MMR Cossim, K-
nearest-neighbors (KNN) Crosscoder, KNN Cossim. The
highest Question Answer (QA) score for Dartboard (see
Table 1) is Exact String Match score of 85.6% (obtained
performing a string match of the response on a set of
correct answers, thus making each response as either correct
or incorrect). Then, the highest Normalized Discounted
Cumulative Gain (NDCG) score is 0.975. An inherent
drawback of Dartboard is its computational complexity and
hyperparameter sensitivity.

Y an et.al. [26] introduced a technique called Corrective
RAG (CRAG) aimed at improving robustness, automatic self-
correction, and the effective exploitation of retrieved docu-
ments in RAG systems. CRAG begins with an initial retrieval
phase in which the user’s query is sent to a retriever to obtain
the top-k documents. Each resulting question-answer pair is
then evaluated by a T5-large-based retrieval evaluator, which
assigns a relevance score and classifies the pair into three
categories: correct, incorrect, or ambiguous. The corrective
procedure unfolds as follows: if the evaluator labels a pair
as correct, the corresponding document is split into small
fragments (‘‘knowledge strips’’); each strip is re-evaluated
and, if deemed irrelevant, discarded, whereas relevant strips
are merged into the internal knowledge store. If a pair is
judged as incorrect, all retrieved documents are considered
useless, the question is rewritten, and a web search is
performed; the newly retrieved information is filtered in the
same way as in the correct phase and stored as external
knowledge. If the evaluator deems a pair ambiguous, the
system combines internal and external knowledge to improve
robustness, after which the generator receives the query

and Self-CRAG, with Self-CRAG incorporated the idea of

First step is Warm-
up: asks a large model such as GPT-4 to rewrite training
questions into sharper search queries. They keep only the
question–query pairs that lead to correct answers and use
these ‘‘pseudo-labels’’ to fine-tune a smaller rewriter model
(T5-large, 770 million parameters) so it can copy the same
query style. Second step is Reinforcement learning: Once the
rewriter is reasonably skilled, it starts writing its own queries. Each query goes to the retriever; the retrieved documents
are passed to a reader LLM, which produces an answer. The system gives a reward based on answer accuracy and
adds a KL-divergence penalty if the rewriter’s style drifts
too far from the original model. Using Proximal Policy
Optimization (PPO), the rewriter’s parameters are updated so
it more often creates queries that steer the reader toward the
correct answer. Multiple datasets, including HotpotQA [42],
AmbigNQ [43], PopQA [33], MMNU [44], were used to
evaluate the suggested approach. The highest Exact Match
score of 45.72 was obtained for PopQA dataset.

This approach offered the benefits of
operational efficiency and enhanced performance. Sun et al. [45], proposed a method known as the Recite-
Read method. Recitation is carried out by giving the LLM
examples of query–support pairs inside the prompt. From
these samples, the model learns in context to recall the
relevant paragraph when it sees a new question, so it can
work without a search engine. Y et a single fact may appear in
several corpora. To avoid depending on one paragraph only,
the method generates several recitations through sampling
and forms a draft answer for each. The system then chooses
the final answer by majority vote. This strategy lowers the
chance of error caused by faulty recitation. The process
is known as Recite-Read. Multiple benchmarks, including
Natural Question [46], Trivia Question [47] and HotpotQA
[42], are employed to evaluate this approach in comparison to
direct questions. Updates are expensive, which is the primary
disadvantage of the Recite-Read method. Deng et al. [48], proposed a method called Credibility-
Aware Attention Modification (CrAM). CrAM is a method
that makes RAG systems aware of source credibility.

Deng et al. [48], proposed a method called Credibility-
Aware Attention Modification (CrAM). CrAM is a method
that makes RAG systems aware of source credibility. It first identifies the attention heads in the LLM that
most strongly influence the model when it accidentally
relies on low-credibility documents to generate incorrect
answers, and then rescales those heads by multiplying each
token’s attention weight by the credibility score of its
source document—trusted sources keep their full weight,
while doubtful ones receive less. This adjustment steers the
model toward reliable information and away from possible
misinformation, improving answer accuracy without the need
to retrain the entire LLM. This approach was evaluated using
Trivia Question [47]. Effectiveness of the CrAM approach
lies in its user-friendly plug-and-play idea, which enhances its
usability. However, the limitation of CrAM is the granularity
of the credibility score.

In the indexing stage, documents are split into smaller
chunks, which are transformed into vector representations
using an embedding function. In this study, we used Sentence-
BERT [52], a transformer-based model that is designed
to produce sentence-level embeddings with high semantic
accuracy. These vector representations are saved in a vector
database to make retrieval process more efficient in the next
steps. When a user makes a query, the first operation performed
by the system is the retrieving stage. In this phase, the
question is processed using the same embedding technique
as in indexing, converting it into a vector representation. A semantic search using similarity measures (e.g., cosine
similarity) is then performed between the vectorized query
and the vectors stored in the database to find the most relevant
chunks. The similarity between each chunk and the query
is calculated, and the results are sorted to select the top-k
chunks. In the generating stage, the retrieved chunks are combined
with the user’s original question and used as input to a
large language model (LLM). The LLM creates a clear and

CONTEXT AWARE RETRIEVAL AUGMENTED
GENERATION
Context Aware Retrieval Augmented Generation (CA-RAG)
operates through three main stages: indexing (III-B1),
generation (III-B2) and post-processing (III-B3). Fig. 2
provides an overview of the workflow of the proposed CA-
RAG system. Unlike traditional RAG, CA-RAG improves
the traditional ‘‘retrieve and read’’ approach with adjustments
in its stages to better handle context-aware tasks, as better
described in the following. 1) INDEXING STAGE
In the indexing stage, documents undergo pre-processing and
chunking processes, in a way similar to the one used in
the traditional RAG workflow. However, as it is highlighted
in [37], traditional chunking often rely on text splitters. While
this method can be effective, text splitters sometimes fails
to keep the semantic meaning of a document during the
chunking process. To solve this problem, a simple semantic
chunking method is proposed in this study. The semantic chunking process, as shown in Algorithm 1,
starts by converting the text (T ) into a list of sentences (S ). 170070 VOLUME 13, 2025

yielded better performance than Technique 1. IV. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULT
In this study, we conducted experiments to evaluate the
performance of the proposed CA-RAG method in two
different scenarios. The first scenario used the TriviaQA[47],
Natural Question [46], AmbigQA [43], and Stanford Ques-
tion Answering Dataset (SQuAD) [50] benchmark dataset,
while the second scenario involved a custom dataset with
questions divided into general, specific, and out-of-context
categories. We made a comparative evaluation among our
proposed approach and multiple RAG configurations using
different retrieval setups: RAG with MiniLM as embedding
model, RAG with Contriever as embedding model, and
additional two configurations applying a Reranker to both of
the two aforementioned embedding setups.

under more realistic conditions, that is including real
documents, such as scientific articles, in order to assess the
capability of the systems of handling much longer contextual
information, where only a part of it may be relevant to specific
questions. Unlike Scenario 1, we used a manual evaluation
method in this case.
In Scenario 2, the evaluation was carried out at the
chunk level and the question level. This means that human
evaluators assessed whether the system generated a correct
or incorrect answer based on the result of the generated
answer obtained from the LLMs model, according to several
conditions. As a result, for each topic with n questions and
m retrieved chunks, the evaluation required assessing n× m
question-chunk pairs. Each pair was evaluated individually,
making the assessment more fine-grained and sensitive to
context.
The manual evaluation for Scenario 2 followed these
criteria: a generated answer which is found to be correct for
specific or general questions has been classified as a True
Positive (TP); when the system provides an incorrect answer
for specific and general questions, this is classified as a False
Positive (FP); the case in which the system correctly responds
with ‘‘no context provided’’ for out-of-context questions is
classified as a True Negative (TN); finally, if the system
provides an answer different from ‘‘no context provided’’ for
out-of-context questions, this is classified as a False Negative
(FN).

The selection of these four datasets is based on specific
considerations regarding the characteristics and challenges
inherent in the Question Answering task. The SQuAD dataset
has been chosen because it focuses on explicit answers within
short contexts, where the answer can be found as a text
span from the provided paragraph. The TriviaQA dataset
serves a similar function to SQuAD, being explicit in answer
retrieval; however, it differs in that it requires cross-sentence
reasoning to obtain the answer, thus involving a larger
context. The Natural Questions dataset has been selected
because it demands deep comprehension and advanced
reasoning skills, extending beyond mere span matching as
seen in SQuAD or cross-sentence matching in TriviaQA.

long documents, Scenario 2 evaluates scientific papers that

In this section, a quantitative and comparative evaluation of
the computational times for the proposed method is provided,
considering Scenario 2 experiments. We selected Scenario
2 because it is more representative of real-world documents. In this context, we provide the average time per question,
as shown in Table 5. According to our results, the proposed
method records an average running time per question
of 262.63s under semantic chunking with the miniLM
embedding, and 262.65s with contriever-msmarco. Under
fixed-size chunking, the average time per question increases
to 2289.47s (miniLM) and 2289.49s (contriever-msmarco),
since fixed-size chunking typically yields a larger number of
chunks than semantic chunking, and this directly translates
into more LLM calls. Compared with the RAG and RAG-
Rerank baselines, our approach entails higher computational

answers reliability. Moreover, under realistic conditions,
a human reader typically needs ∼ 70–80s per question to
read, locate significant content, and synthesize an answer
from a short document (up to 200 words) [64]. Assuming,
conservatively, linear scaling with document length, this cor-

2 documents range from a minimum of∼ 6700 to a maximum
of ∼ 11200 words, the time required to read and provide
an answer would be approximately 2345–3920s (i.e., about
39-65 minutes) under the most optimistic rate of 0.35 s/word. This should be considered as a conservative upper bound,
which could be appropriate for the first question, while
for subsequent questions the reader typically can reuse
previously acquired knowledge and only consult specific
sections, thus the incremental per-question time could be
lower. Our comparison should therefore be interpreted as

Augmented Generation called Context-Aware Retrieval Aug-
mented Generation (CA-RAG), which adapts the ‘‘retrieve
and read’’ framework used by traditional RAG while
eliminating vector representations and the top-k process in
the retrieve stage. The approach incorporates a similarity

and read’’ framework used by traditional RAG while
eliminating vector representations and the top-k process in
the retrieve stage. The approach incorporates a similarity
evaluator after the generative phase to address hallucination
issues and enhance contextual relevance. The choice of either
cosine similarity or dot product between the embedding of the

both RAG and CA-RAG without post-processing, achieving

method’s ability to detect correctly when there is no relevant

Negatives (TN) and fewer False Positives (FP) and False
Negative (FN). In contrast, models without post-processing
often produced hallucinated answers, as they lacked a
mechanism to filter out irrelevant chunks. These results
highlight the importance of post-processing techniques in
generative QA, particularly when operating in complex,
open-domain environments where questions may not always
align with the retrieved content.

Ghofran Khalaf
 , May Itani
 , Member , IEEE, and Sanaa Sharafeddine

Abstract—Digital Twin (DT) technology has emerged as a
promising link between the physical and virtual worlds, enabling
simulation, prediction, and real-time performance optimization in
different domains. In this work we develop a high-ﬁdelity digital
twin framework, focusing on synchronization and accuracy
between physical and digital systems to enhance data-driven
decision making. To achieve this, we deploy several stationary
UA Vs in optimized locations to collect data from IoT devices,
which were used to monitor multiple physical entities and
perform computations to evaluate their status. We formulate a
mixed-integer non-convex program to maximize the total amount
of data collected from all IoT devices while ensuring a constrained
age of digital twin threshold and solve it using successive convex
approximation (SCA). To cope with realistic scenarios involving
unpredictable environments and large network sizes, we model
our problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), and propose
a deep reinforcement learning-based approach using a Twin
Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) to optimize

involved. According to [5] and [6], the main challenges include
data acquisition and processing, high-ﬁdelity modeling, and
real-time communication between virtual and real twins. The
precision and efﬁciency of data collection signiﬁcantly affect
the quality of the DT model [7]. Since a large amount of
real-time data is required to establish a high-ﬁdelity digital
twin [5], IoT devices often fail to deliver their real-time
measurements to the base station due to limited transmit power
and processing capacity. Utilizing uncrewed aerial vehicles
(UA Vs) to collect and process data from IoT devices offers
a reliable and affordable wireless connectivity solution and is
widely adopted in similar problem setup [8], [9], [10], [11].

ital twins. On one hand, synchronization can be improved
by reducing the Age of Digital Twin (AoDT) metric. This
synchronization metric measures the time gap between the
current status of the monitored physical entity and its digital
counterpart. AoDT was ﬁrst introduced in [12] and is based
on the AoI, which reﬂects information freshness and was
ﬁrst introduced in 2010 [13]. Thus, AoDT measures status
freshness to determine whether the digital twin accurately
mirrors the current condition of a given physical entity. On

3014 IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON NETWORK AND SERVICE MANAGEMENT, VOL. 23, 2026
optimizes a DT-aided IoT network by balancing accuracy and
synchronization. We consider a system composed of several physical entities,
each monitored by a group of IoT devices. UA Vs are deployed
to collect measurements from all IoT devices and process them
to determine the status of the physical entities in the system. Our work utilizes the novel AoDT metric, which accounts
for both upload and processing of sensitive data through
employment of UA Vs as edge devices to provide computing
services and efﬁcient data collection and transmission to the
base station. We derive a closed-form expression for the
AoDT metric to reﬂect the status freshness of the digital twin.

We then formulate a mixed-integer non-convex optimization
problem to maximize DT accuracy while maintaining syn-
chronization and solve the problem using successive convex
approximations (SCA). We propose a more efﬁcient and
scalable solution using reinforcement learning, speciﬁcally
twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) solution
approach. Extensive simulations validate the effectiveness of
the SCA-based and TD3-based approaches. To the best of our
knowledge, no research work has tackled a similar problem
with IoT devices sending fresh status updates to the digital
twin platform to build a highly synchronized and accurate
digital twin, with each physical entity being monitored by
multiple IoT devices.

all collected measurements to determine the status of the
monitored physical entities and deliver this information
to the digital twin running at the base station for system
monitoring and management. 2) We derive a closed form expression for the novel AoDT

at (xBS,yBS, zBS). A set of I IoT devices, denoted by

such as temperature, pressure, humidity, vibration, ﬂow rate,
and others, of the components of the system, named physical
entities. Due to their limited transmission power and lack of
processing capabilities, IoT devices deliver their readings to a

that are optimally positioned at the coordinates (xj,yj,H ),

Modeling Quality of Service in a Digital Twin
Many research is emerging to deﬁne methods and met-
rics for evaluating digital twin performance. Authors in [35]
illustrated that ensuring real-time synchronization between
a DT and its physical counterpart as well as maintaining
high accuracy in a DT is crucial for effective DT adoption
in different applications. Authors in [36] introduced digital
twin entanglement metric that represents to which extent the
digital and physical systems’ synchronization process fulﬁlls
the needs of a speciﬁc application. Authors took into account
the freshness of the collected data and the ratio of collected
to total data. This ratio reﬂects the DT accuracy. Moreover,
authors in [37] illustrated that DT freshness may be deﬁned
using the age of information concept as the elapsed time after
a DT has been updated. However, they did not derive any
closed formula to model this metric. DT freshness can be

using the age of information concept as the elapsed time after
a DT has been updated. However, they did not derive any
closed formula to model this metric. DT freshness can be
best represented through a novel metric introduced in [12] as
age of digital twin metric (AoDT) that takes into account: (i)
time of data upload from sensors to edge device; (ii) time of
data processing to reﬂect device status; and (iii) time of data
download to BS for DT updates. Authors in [12] considered a
simple scenario where one IoT monitors one physical process. They proposed a problem to optimize DT accuracy subject to
AoDT constraints. However; in practice, multiple IoT devices
might monitor the same physical entity.

In this work, we
formulate a closed form expression to model age of digital
twin in such a practical scenario. The age of information (AoI) is a destination-centric mea-
sure for information freshness that counts the time that has
passed since the last fresh update was generated at the source. In this study, we apply the concept of AoI to the setting of
digital twins, where we need to express the freshness of the
physical entity’s status through the responsive DT. As a result,
we utilize the Age of Digital Twin (AoDT) metric introduced
in [12] and deﬁned as the elapsed time between data generation
and the status update received by the BS. The calculation of the AoDT for each monitored process
accounts for different phases after data collection, namely:

accounts for different phases after data collection, namely:
• Upload phase: The data is transmitted to the associated
UA V through the wireless channel for processing, and
then forwarded from the associated UA V to another one
when the ﬁrst UA V lacks computation resources. • Processing phase: The uploaded data enters the compu-
tation queue at the UA V and is then processed to obtain
results. • Download phase: The data is processed from the UA V to
the BS via the LoS channel to update the DT’s status.

VI. T WIN DELAYED DEEP DETERMINISTIC POLICY
GRADIENT -BASED SOLUTION APPROACH
In UA V-assisted IoT networks with DT functionality, real-
time decision-making and dynamic optimization are crucial
in maximizing data collection efﬁciency while maintaining
AoDT constraints. Owing to the complexity of the optimiza-
tion problem due to its nonconvex constraints and to cope
with uncertainty and to ensure real time adaptability especially
in dynamic environments, we resort to deep reinforcement
learning (DRL) as a viable solution approach [23].
The standard DDPG algorithm occasionally encounters
instability and hyperparameter sensitivity, due to Q-value
overestimation, and hence produces a non-optimal or divergent

scenarios. Therefore, in our work, we adopt the TD3 algo-
rithm, an off-policy actor-critic method that extends the DDPG
framework to continuous action spaces. It learns a deter-
ministic policy using two Q-value critics to estimate the
optimal policy value while addressing value-function overes-
timation bias. This is achieved through three key techniques:
clipped Double Q-learning, delayed policy updates, and tar-
get policy smoothing. The most crucial one is the clipped
Double Q-Learning technique, which trains two independent
Q-networks in parallel and uses the lower estimate as the
target value to enhance stability and robustness.

A DRL approach based on the TD3 algorithm is proposed
for ﬁnding the policy that optimizes UA V positioning, IoT-
to-UA V assignment, and edge-computation scheduling under
unknown activation patterns. We customize TD3 to our frame-
work by redeﬁning the state S, action A, and reward R
functions as follows:
• State: The state space of our TD3-based reinforcement
learning algorithm is deﬁned by the initial positions
of UA Vs and IoT devices, task arrival rate, allocated
bandwidth for the whole system, current load on UA V j,
average AoDT, and communication channel conditions.

requirements. Fig. 3 presents our system architecture, divided into three
interconnected components. On the left, the RL Module
includes the actor-critic pair: the actor proposes continuous
control commands (UA V motion deltas, IoT-UA V associations
and bandwidth allocations) which are evaluated by two critic
networks. Then, the experience tuples are stored in a replay
buffer and used, along with clipped target actions from slowly
updated target networks, to perform off-policy learning. In
the middle, the digital model simulates the environment state,
including UA V and IoT locations, task arrival rates, allocated
resources and resulting communication metrics, and computes
the scalar reward by aggregating throughput, AoDT penalties,
distance penalties, and constraint violations. Finally, on the
right, the physical entities depict the UA V ﬂeet and IoT devices
executing the digital model’s commands and feeding back
sensor data, thus completing the cycle from perception to
action. B. RL Algorithm

presented in Algorithm 2 to optimize UA V placement and task
ofﬂoading under AoDT constraints in a continuously evolving
environment. We train a TD3 agent where at each time step
t the agent observes a high-dimensional state st (including
UA V/IoT positions, group assignments, loads, AoDT values,
and bandwidths) and selects a continuous action at (UA V

C ONCLUSION
DT technology serves as a vital tool in real-time network
monitoring and performance optimization [41]. In this work,
we addressed the problem of developing a highly synchronized
and highly accurate digital twin of a physical system by
leveraging multiple UA Vs positioned in optimized locations
to collect and process data from a ﬁeld of IoT devices used to
monitor multiple processes in the given system. Our problem
considered the practical case where a group of multiple IoT
devices monitors the same physical process. We formulated the
problem as a mixed-integer non-convex program to optimize
the total sum rate of IoT devices, resource allocation, and UA V
postioning, while ensuring a constrained AoDT that reﬂects the
digital twin data freshness. We solve the problem using succes-
sive convex approximations and propose a more efﬁcient and
scalable learning-based solution. To do so, we model the prob-
lem as MDP and solve it using twin delayed deep deterministic

demonstrate the performance superiority of the TD3-based

Adaptive Trust Architecture for Secure IoT Communication in 6G
Ijaz Ahmad , Graduate Student Member, IEEE , Shakthi Gimhana , Graduate Student Member, IEEE ,
Ijaz Ahmad , Senior Member, IEEE, and Erkki Harjula , Member, IEEE
Abstract—This letter presents an adaptive trust architecture
that enables secure, low-latency communication in 6G-enabled
Internet of Things (IoT) networks, centering around a novel
Adaptive Zero Trust Manager (AZTM) deployed at the network
edge.

common attacks, and suitability for mission-critical 6G applica-

I. I NTRODUCTION
T
HE RAPID expansion of the IoT is driving transformative
applications in latency-sensitive 6G verticals, including
vehicular networks, industrial automation, and healthcare. With its promises of ultra-low latency, massive connectivity,
and energy efﬁciency, the evolution of 6G presents new
opportunities alongside complex security challenges [1].T h e
massive scale and heterogeneity of IoT deployments demand
adaptive security mechanisms that can maintain trust in
dynamic, distributed environments. 6G will emphasize decen-
tralization, AI-powered automation [2], and sustainability
necessitating lightweight, scalable, and autonomous security
frameworks.

We illustrate the architecture through a healthcare IoT
scenario, where edge-connected devices (e.g., wearables
and sensors) securely exchange sensitive data. In such
latency-sensitive environments, continuous authentication and
dynamic trust enforcement are essential to prevent threats such
as replay or impersonation. The proposed architecture centers
on the AZTM, deployed at the Tier-1 edge, which performs
three critical functions:
1) Behavior-Aware Trust Evaluation:Continuously updates
node trust scores based on real-time behavioral obser-
vations (e.g., frequency of interactions, compliance,
anomalies). 2) Consensus-Free Trust Logging: Integrates with a
lightweight blockchain ledger to immutably log interac-
tions, trust decisions and node status, without requiring
energy-intensive consensus. 3) Secure Key Exchange: Employs ECDH for symmetric
key derivation, eliminating pre-shared secrets and sup-
porting scalable direct communication. AZTM acts as the policy enforcer and trust anchor within
the system, ofﬂoading complexity from constrained IoT nodes
while maintaining continuous veriﬁcation. By combining zero

key management, the module enables fast, secure authentica-

AZTM is the core of our architecture. It evaluates node
behavior, updates trust scores, initiates key exchanges, and
ensures tamper-proof logging. Behavior-Driven Trust Scoring: Each node begins with an
initial trust score of 50. As shown in Algorithm 2, trust scores
are adjusted based on observed behavior: penalties for actions
like self-vouching, Sybil attempts, or DoS patterns; rewards for
successful authenticated communication; and decay for inac-
tivity beyond a conﬁgurable threshold. Behavior is assessed at
run-time based on event logs. Trust State Management and Logging: Trust values
are maintained as JSON objects in the RPi memory and
periodically logged to a lightweight blockchain for immutabil-
ity. Unlike traditional consensus mechanisms, our system
eliminates overhead by assigning trust update authority to the
edge node, which signs updates using its private key.

IV . SECURITY ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION
AZTM plays a central role in enforcing security within the
proposed architecture. It continuously monitors node behav-
ior, assigns or revokes trust based on predeﬁned policies,
and enables secure peer interactions through dynamic key
exchange. This section demonstrates how AZTM effectively
mitigates common IoT threats, ensures fairness across diverse
node proﬁles, and maintains operational efﬁciency in real-time
6G environments.

Trust Score Dynamics
Fig. 3 illustrates the evolution of trust scores under
three behavioral categories: malicious, honest, and inactive. Malicious nodes, which exhibit behaviors such as self-
vouching or repeated re-registration (indicative of Sybil or
DoS attacks), face progressive trust penalties and eventual
exclusion. Honest nodes receive steady trust rewards for
consistent, authenticated participation. Inactive nodes experi-
ence gradual trust decay, encouraging active and accountable
participation without harsh penalties. These dynamics validate
AZTM‘s ability to enforce policy while adapting to node
behavior in real time. B. Energy-Aware Trust Enforcement
Trust evaluation and key exchange processes incur minimal
energy overhead, as shown in Figs. 4 and 5. ESP32 nodes
show brief energy spikes during cryptographic operations, but
these are infrequent due to session-based ECDH exchanges. AZTM optimizes performance by avoiding consensus mecha-
nisms and by limiting trust evaluations to behavioral triggers. The RPi‘s energy proﬁle remains stable during logging and
trust computations, validating the system’s suitability for low-
power environments. C. Behavior-Driven Threat Mitigation

ONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
This letter introduced an Adaptive Zero Trust Manager
(AZTM) deployed at the local edge to enable secure, low-
latency communication in 6G-enabled IoT environments. By combining zero trust principles with a consensus-free
blockchain and behavior-driven trust scoring, AZTM enforces
real-time authentication, eliminate single point of failure and
lightweight policy compliance. The system supports secure
key exchange using ECDH and mitigates dynamic threats
through continuous trust evaluation. Experimental results
